steps: Permit & prep
Check restrictions, installation requirements and permit needs with the local authority having jurisdiction. Take the doors off until all finishing work around the fireplace is complete.

Check with the local authority having jurisdiction (building department, fire department, fire prevention bureau) about restrictions, installation requirements and the need for a permit.

Remove the doors until all finishing work around the fireplace is done, to avoid scratches or damage from drywall dust, muriatic acid, plaster, cement, paint or other sprays and liquids.

RSF strongly recommends installation and service by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada). The listing label is glued to the bottom of the fireplace; remove the bottom louver to read it.
Location & ceiling height

Plan fireplace, chimney and options together; avoid cutting roof and floor joists, and run the chimney inside the house if possible (outside: insulated chase). No special floor reinforcement is needed.

Plan the whole installation (fireplace, chimney, options) before starting. Choose a location that doesn't require cutting roof or floor joists. Run the chimney up through the inside of the house if at all possible; if it must run outside, enclose it in an insulated chase. A cold chimney causes poor draft.

Min. ceiling height, sealed enclosure7'
Min. ceiling height, vented enclosure6'

Measured from the base of the fireplace; applies to all ceilings above it (room ceiling, enclosure ceiling). A vented enclosure needs regular 3"x10" or larger grilles in holes cut within 1" of both the floor and the ceiling, placed vertically or horizontally.

Never pack required air spaces with insulation or other materials.
Secure to the floor
The fireplace must be attached to the floor: reuse the four crate brackets, placed as they were on the crate, with at least one screwed into a floor joist with 2" wood screws if possible.
Install the standoffs

Before installing the fireplace, screw the top standoff (centered) and both side standoffs to the casing with the self-tapping screws provided, bent edge flush with the facing. Seal the ¼" gap at the top standoffs with high-temperature sealant and fill nothing behind it.
Frame the enclosure

Combustibles no closer than the standoffs at top, back and sides; keep a 2" open space around the chimney from the fireplace up to the ceiling (no firestop there). The ceiling firestop is never closer to the fireplace base than Table 1 (C).

Frame with any suitable material (2"x4" or 2"x6" studs, plywood, gypsum board). Combustible materials must not go closer to the fireplace than the standoffs on the top, back and sides. You may completely cover the top as long as all standoff clearances and the 2" clearance around the chased chimney are kept.

Leave the 2" space around the chimney open from the fireplace up to the ceiling (no firestop). The distance from the ceiling firestop to the fireplace base must never be less than Table 1 (C): 7' sealed, 6' vented enclosure.

Recommended framing dimensions are shown as a drawing (Figure 6) on this page; the manual notes they are larger than required for ease of installation.
Outside air duct

With the fireplace in position, run insulated aluminium flexible duct rated over 200°F (93°C) to the outside inlet: 4" for total runs under 25', 5" beyond, max. 12' vertical rise. The inlet sits at least 5' below the rain cap and never in an attic.

1. Pick a location for the duct and inlet; the inlet can be above or below floor level.
  2. Cut a 4 ¼" hole (5 ¼" for 5" duct) in the outside wall, push the inlet in from outside and seal the joint.
  3. Fit the duct over the inlet's round sleeve. At both ends pull back the insulation and plastic cover, attach the duct with metal screws, push the cover back and tape it with 2" aluminium duct tape.

Loop the duct for an optional cold air trap, and don't crimp it at corners. Suggested kit: 4" RSF outside air kit (FO-INT). Both 4" and 5" connecting sleeves come with the fireplace.
Chimney through floors & roof

8" ICC EXCEL only: 14" square rough openings, a radiation shield under each floor, a radiation shield and storm collar at the attic, and the first length fixed to the fireplace with the three screws provided. Finish with flashing, storm collar and rain cap.

1. Cut and frame 14" square openings (slightly larger is fine, never smaller) in floors, ceilings and roof.
  2. From below, install a radiation shield in each floor; at the attic, a radiation shield and a storm collar.
  3. Place the first length on the fireplace and secure it with the three screws provided. The chimney must extend at least 3' above its point of contact with the roof and at least 2' higher than any wall, roof or building within 10'. Over 5' above the roof, secure it with a roof brace.
  4. Flashing, if the chimney is enclosed to the roof: vented flashing in the USA; vented flashing, or a roof radiation shield with regular flashing, in Canada. Seal it with roofing tar or exterior sealant, under the upper shingles and over the lower ones, and fasten with roofing nails or screws. Never block the vented flashing's openings.
  5. Storm collar: a bead of clear or grey exterior sealant below, pull the collar through it, then seal again on top (not roofing tar).
  6. Fit the rain cap and secure it with the screws provided.
Keep 2" or more between the chimney and combustible material, and don't fill it with insulation. The fireplace supports a maximum of 16' of chimney.
Offsets & chase (if needed)

Max. offset 30° (USA) / 45° (Canada) and max. four elbows; 3 metal screws per joint and a wall or offset support above each offset. A chimney run outside goes in an insulated chase built as an extension of the home.

An elbow may go directly on top of the fireplace. Use the offset charts in the EXCEL chimney installation manual. Install the elbow, enough lengths for the offset and a return elbow, securing each joint with 3 metal screws, then a wall support or offset support above each offset (elbows don't support the chimney above).

Through an exterior wall at an angle: use an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-8EWRSI30 or XM-8EWRSI45), and leave off its outside plate if the chimney is enclosed outside. Check the ceiling height.

Chase: insulate between the footings and the floor; in a mild climate at least to the first firestop, in a very cold climate to the top. Insulate the chase ceiling as for an attic. Insulated, vapor-sealed walls sheathed with fire rated gypsum board are strongly recommended (some codes require them); if you do this, don't insulate the wall above the front of the fireplace.
Masonry chimney (if used)

Run EXCEL chimney from the fireplace top to a listed stainless liner (EXCEL, or ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777) fitted inside the clay liner to the top, joined with the FO-FDM8 masonry adapter. Use at least one 18" EXCEL length after the elbow, 12" min. from the ceiling.

An existing masonry chimney must first be inspected by an authority having jurisdiction: well built and fully lined per local codes and NBC or NFPA 211, cleaned of soot and creosote and in good condition, no insulation touching it or inside it, all clearances respected along its full run, and used for this fireplace only. If major repairs are needed, build a new chimney.

The stainless liner doesn't replace the clay liner. FO-FDM8 attaches to the liner with 3 stainless steel rivets and to the EXCEL chimney with 3 screws (provided); after mortaring, the joint should not be visible. Open the masonry from the center out, keeping three sides of the clay liner in place.

If a rigid liner is hard to fit, or the chimney is less than 10"x10" inside, use a listed flexible stainless liner with the LM-8LAF flexible/rigid adaptor. In a new chimney built around a 6"x10" clay liner, the stainless liner must be ovalized.
Facing, hearth & mantel

Non-combustible facing only (gypsum board stays outside the standoffs); keep door swing and never block the louvers or side openings. Hearth extension 18" deep and 40" wide with the spark guard; combustible mantel shelf 12" deep max., 24" min. above the opening.

Facing must be non-combustible, such as metal, brick, slate or ceramic tile; painted cement board or ceramic tile glued with high temperature silicone works. Gypsum board is not an acceptable facing and can't be closer than the side and top standoffs. Leave room for the doors to open, and don't cover or block any part of the louvers or the openings on each side of the firebox.

Hearth: non-combustible (brick, tile, stone, slate), at least 18" deep from the front and 40" total width centered on the firebox opening; no minimum thickness. Install the spark guard as described under the hearth spec.

Mantel: combustible shelf at most 12" deep, its bottom at least 24" above the top of the firebox opening. Combustible posts of any depth may sit at the side-wall distance.

panels.title: Smoke when the door opens
items: Door opened too quickly → open it more slowly
Dirty chimney or plugged cap → screened caps clog with creosote
Chimney too short for the altitude and number of elbows (Table 2)
Range hood or bathroom exhaust fan running → house pressure
Pressure imbalance → open a window near the fireplace a little
Too little kindling → smoke is most likely while lighting

panels.title: Weak draft
items: Smoke entering the room; hard to light or operate
Often wrongly blamed on a blocked air intake
Most common fix: add chimney height
Cold chimney run outside → enclose it in an insulated chase
Severely depressurized house → outside air won't stop smoking

panels.title: Excessive draft / over-firing
items: Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burn times, less heat recovery
Burn rate won't slow, or the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red
Poorly adjusted door seal → over-firing, excess wood use, premature failure
Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste

panels.title: Poor fire or dirty glass
items: Wet wood → hard to burn, little heat, more creosote, dark glass deposits
Outside air damper closed → fire may be starved for air
Fire goes out after closing the door → door shut too early
Slow fires leave deposits → a good hot fire once a day; wax firelogs dirty the glass

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Read the manual before your first fire. Then:

  1. Make sure the outside air damper is open.
  2. Crumple newspaper as your fire starter. Use enough to light the kindling; 5-6 pieces should do.
  3. Lay the kindling crisscrossed over the paper. Plenty of kindling heats the chimney quickly and builds a strong draft.
  4. Light the paper. Partially close one of the doors, but don't shut it completely. When the door is in the right spot, you'll see air rushing into the fireplace.
  5. Once the kindling is burning on its own, add small pieces of seasoned cordwood, always at least 3. Use the andirons on either side so the wood doesn't flatten and smother the fire. Set the pieces so the rising fire hits several of them and has air gaps to flow through.
  6. Keep one door slightly open until the cordwood is lit. Close the door completely once the fire is established.
Fire went out? The door was closed too early.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids. Don't use a grate or raise the fire. Keep the fire behind the andirons, and move any log that falls against the glass.
Note: p. 6 says setting the outside air control lever horizontal completely opens the outside air damper; p. 9, in its steps for removing the bottom louver, calls horizontal the lever's closed position.
Note: p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the doors fully closed, because a door left partly open can draw gas and flame out of the opening, creating fire and smoke hazards; p. 7's steps for lighting and reloading leave one door slightly open until the wood is lit (about 3-10 minutes when reloading).

firstfires.title: Your first fires
firstfires.html:
Expect a slow start-up during the first few fires. That's normal.

Black bricks

The refractory bricks lining the firebox still hold moisture from manufacturing. It takes a few hot fires to dry them out. Until then they look black with smoke deposits. Once the moisture is gone, they turn white.

No break-in fires needed

Unlike a cast iron stove, this fireplace doesn't need curing with small fires that slowly get bigger. Feel free to light a large fire from the very start.

A slight smell

You'll notice an odor during the first few fires. It comes from the paint curing and oil burning off the metal. It may be strong enough to set off your smoke detector. Open the doors and windows so the room can air out.

control.title: Controlling the heat
control.html:
The Focus ST has no draft control. You set how hard it burns with the size and placement of the logs.

For a cooler, lazy fire

Load 2 to 3 large logs in the center of the hearth, between the andirons, with their sides facing you (not the ends).

For a warmer, brighter fire

Load a number of small logs with the ends facing you, so one end comes very close to the glass. Put half of them near one glass and half near the other. The combustion air comes in near the glass, so this makes a more vigorous fire.

How it burns

It burns at a fixed rate that depends on the heat inside the firebox: fast while it lights up, then gradually slower for the best efficiency and emissions reduction. Faster fires make more heat, but more of it goes up the chimney and they use much more wood.

The door seal matters most. A good door gasket seal is the most important factor in controlling the burn rate. To check it, latch the door on a sheet of paper and pull gently but firmly. If the paper tears or is hard to pull out, the seal is right. Check all sides. Replace a worn gasket; kits are available from your RSF dealer.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
1. Have your next load of wood ready before you open the door. The firebox cools quickly while the door is open, but don't rush.
  2. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room.
  3. Poke and stir the unburnt wood left in the firebox to revive the fire, then place the new logs.
  4. Keep the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes, depending on how well seasoned the wood is and how many coals were left. Close it once the new wood is well lit.
Note: p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the doors fully closed, because a door left partly open can draw gas and flame out of the opening, creating fire and smoke hazards; p. 7's steps for lighting and reloading leave one door slightly open until the wood is lit (about 3-10 minutes when reloading).

Smoke coming into the room?

  • Open the door more slowly. Opening it quickly creates a suction of air into the room.
  • Turn off kitchen range hoods and bathroom exhaust fans. They create negative pressure that pulls smoke out of the fireplace.
  • Open a window near the fireplace a little to equalize the pressure. Close it once the draft is established.
  • Make sure the chimney is clean and the cap isn't plugged. Caps with screens clog with creosote more easily.
  • Use enough kindling to get a hot fire going quickly. Smoke is most likely to come in while you're lighting the fire.

air.title: The outside air control
air.html:
The fireplace burns air from both inside and outside your home. Room air comes in through an opening at the bottom of both doors. Outside air comes in through the connection on the side of the fireplace when the outside air damper is open. The control lever is housed in a bottom louver.

  • Open it to burn. RSF recommends always using outside air for combustion. Cold, dense outside air helps start the fire. If you don't open the damper while burning wood, the fire may be starved for air.
  • Close it when the fireplace isn't burning, so cold outside air doesn't come into your home.
  • You can choose to burn with room air instead.
  • Outside air can help with negative pressure in the house, but it won't stop the fireplace from smoking in a severely depressurized house.
Note: p. 6 says setting the outside air control lever horizontal completely opens the outside air damper; p. 9, in its steps for removing the bottom louver, calls horizontal the lever's closed position.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn seasoned cordwood: wood that's been cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood is generally under 20% moisture. A combination of densified fuel logs and wood is also allowed.

Wet wood is hard to burn. It gives lower efficiency, more creosote and dark deposits on the glass, and you can burn a lot of it and get very little heat.

All wood gives about the same heat per pound. Hardwood is denser, so more weight fits in the firebox and it burns longer and more evenly.

Never burn

  • Scrap, driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage or plastic.
  • Construction scraps (like 2x4 or plywood) as your only fuel. They can overheat and seriously damage the fireplace.
  • Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste. They can over-fire the fireplace, or start a chimney fire if the flue is dirty.
Note: p. 6 says never to burn scrap; p. 3 says not to use construction scraps (such as 2x4 or plywood scraps) as your only supply of fuel.

Fire logs

Wax fire logs (like Duraflame) aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use wax or densified firelogs, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use, and read their warnings first.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
In a slow-burning fireplace, the glass won't always stay perfectly clean. A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most of the deposits. The drier the wood, the cleaner the glass.

  • Clean the glass only when it's cool. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  • Never use an abrasive cleaner. Use only a cleaner your dealer recommends. Wood stove glass cleaners work far better than regular glass or oven cleaners.
  • Heat won't break the glass, but impact can. Don't hit it, and don't slam the doors.

Protect the paint

Don't spray glass cleaner or other cleaners on the paint. They can strip it and make touch-ups hard. Clean painted parts with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water, never an abrasive cleaner.

To touch up the face, use Stove Bright Metallic Black high temperature paint and follow the can's directions. Never paint while the fireplace is still warm, keep the can away from heat and flame, and ventilate the room until the paint is dry. If you take the glass out of the door, the gasket has to be replaced.

chimney.title: Chimney, creosote & ashes
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapors that mix with moisture from the wood and condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire.

  • Check the chimney for creosote every week or so, until you learn how often it needs cleaning.
  • Soot or creosote 1/8" (3mm) thick or more means clean it right away. You may also need to change how you burn and inspect more often.
  • Close the fireplace doors before sweeping. Use an 8" round brush.

Ashes

  • Remove ashes before they get deep enough to spill out when you open a door.
  • Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  • Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  • If you'll bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders are thoroughly cool.
RSF strongly recommends having the fireplace installed and serviced by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• Operate the fireplace with the doors fully closed. A door left partly open can draw gas and flame out of the opening, creating fire and smoke hazards.
  • Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of your home, and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire, and keep them well away while it's in use.
  • Don't use a grate or other products not specified for this fireplace. Don't add a flue damper, and don't install an insert in it.
  • Don't slam the doors; the glass can break.
Note: p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the doors fully closed, because a door left partly open can draw gas and flame out of the opening, creating fire and smoke hazards; p. 7's steps for lighting and reloading leave one door slightly open until the wood is lit (about 3-10 minutes when reloading).

Signs of over-firing

Don't over-fire the fireplace. You're over-firing if you can't slow down the burn rate, or if the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Damage from over-firing isn't covered by the warranty.

No unvented gas logs. This fireplace hasn't been tested with an unvented gas log set. Never install one.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF Woodburning Fireplaces warrants the fireplace against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, on these terms:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Second through fifth yearsDefective parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Sixth through thirtieth yearsReplacement parts, if available, at 50% of the published retail price; no labor

Not covered

  • Electrical components after the first year (they're covered for one year only)
  • Glass and plating
  • Normal wear and tear, such as paint discoloration, worn gaskets, or eroded or cracked refractory
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or not servicing the unit
  • Repairs not authorized by RSF in advance, freight on replacement parts, and damage in transit
  • Installations that don't meet the manual's requirements
The warranty isn't transferable. Defective parts are repaired or replaced when returned to an authorized RSF dealer. Use only genuine RSF parts: substitutes void the warranty and may put your safety at risk. This is a summary; the full terms are in the manual.

specClear.title: Clearances
specClear.html:
Combustibles to side, back and top standoffs (A)0" (0,0 mm)
Side wall to side of firebox opening (B)9" (229 mm)
Min. ceiling height, sealed enclosure (C)7' (2,13 m)
Min. ceiling height, vented enclosure (C)6' (1,83 m)
Chimney to combustibles2" or more

At 9" (B) the door can't open fully; push the side wall back at least an additional 10" for a full swing. Ceiling height (C) runs from the base of the fireplace to the lowest point of any ceiling above it, inside and outside the enclosure. A vented enclosure needs regular 3"x10" or larger grilles in holes cut within 1" of both floor and ceiling.

Combustibles never go closer than the standoffs on the top, back and sides. Keep the 2" chimney space open and never pack required air spaces with insulation. In the room, combustibles stay at least 4' from the front.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension & spark guard
specHearth.html:
Min. depth from front of fireplace (G)18" (457 mm)
Min. total width, centered on opening (H)40" (1,02 m)
Min. spark guard width (I)36" (914 mm)
Hearth extension thicknessno minimum

Use non-combustible material such as brick, tile, stone or slate. The spark guard provided (5" x 36" sheet metal) goes halfway under the fireplace and halfway under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening, extending 2½" beneath the fireplace. It isn't required on a non-combustible floor.

Raised installations need a site-built guard. Z-shaped when the fireplace bottom is 2 ½" or less above the hearth extension's non-combustible flooring: its height equals the floor-to-base distance and it goes at least 2½" under both. Right-angle when higher than 2 ½": sides at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material. Any custom guard meets the (I) width and is centered on the door opening.

specMantel.title: Mantel
specMantel.html:
Max. combustible shelf depth (J)12" (305 mm)
Min. height, top of firebox opening to bottom of combustible shelf (K)24" (610 mm)

Combustible mantel posts of any depth may go on either side if they keep the side-wall distance (B, 9"). Masonry and other non-combustible shelves can sit directly above the top of the fireplace facing or higher; below the combustible minimum, the wall framing and facing between the top of the metal face and the shelf bottom must be non-combustible.

specFlue.title: Chimney
specFlue.html:
Chimney8" ICC Model EXCEL only

Raise the minimum by approximately 6" for every 1000' of elevation; every 15°, 30° or 45° offset (one pair of elbows) adds more. Table 2 minimum flue heights, measured from the top of the fireplace to the top of the chimney before the rain cap:

0 - 1000 ft · straight / 1 x 30° / 2 x 30°12' / 15' / 18'
1001 - 2000 ft · straight / 1 x 30° / 2 x 30°12'6" / 15'6" / 19'
6001 - 7000 ft · straight / 1 x 30°15' / 18'6"

With two different offsets, use the two-offset column of the biggest pair. The full table (to 10000 ft, with 15° and 45° columns) is on this page. Follow the EXCEL chimney installation manual for supports, bracing and anchors.

specGas.title: Vented gas log option
specGas.html:
Max. gas log set40,000 BTU/h
Log set listingANSI Z21.60/CSA 2.26
Gas line entry1 ¼" hole each side, about 12 ¾" up
Firebox floor air holesfour, 1" diameter, 6" apart center to center
The maximum gas output allowed in the Focus ST is 40,000 BTU/h. The gas log has to be listed to ANSI Z21.60/CSA 2.26.

Vented sets only; the fireplace hasn't been tested with an unvented set. Remove both bottom refractory bricks and store them (everything goes back in to burn wood again). Drill the holes in line, parallel to and halfway between both doors, centered between the side bricks, and leave them completely open. Clean the gray sealant out of the hole in the right side refractory bricks (2) on the chosen side.

RSF requires no minimum clearance from the firebox sides or top to the log set, but the log maker's clearances apply; the gas valve may go inside the firebox if the log maker allows it. Gas line by qualified personnel, per local ordinances and the appropriate Gas Code.

specOptions.title: Options
specOptions.html:

Gravity vent kits duct hot air to a room above or on the same level as the fireplace; each includes 5' of insulated flexible ducting, a fireplace adapter, an outlet grill adapter and a decorative outlet grill. The rock retainer kit is for thin non-combustible facings such as ceramic tile or sliced brick, not full brick or stone; thin materials can also be glued on with high temperature silicone. Instructions come in the box with each option.

Scrap: p. 6 says never to burn scrap (with garbage, treated wood and driftwood); p. 3 says not to use construction scraps (e.g. 2x4 or plywood scraps) as your only supply of fuel. Scrap added to the never-burn list and flagged in the wood drawer.

Doors: p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the doors fully closed, as a partly open door can draw gas and flame out of the opening, creating fire and smoke hazards; p. 7's lighting and refuelling steps leave one door slightly open until the cordwood is lit, and ajar for about 3-10 minutes when refuelling. Flagged in the safety, light and reload drawers.

review.notes: One combined owner's / installation manual. It names no listing standard for the fireplace itself (only ANSI Z21.60/CSA 2.26 for gas logs, ANSI/CAN/UL/ULC 2115 for firelogs and ULC-S635 / ULC-S640 / UL-1777 for liners), so certification is omitted. The manual gives no heat output, efficiency, emissions figure, firebox volume, log length, weight, heating area, view area or mobile-home approval, so those catalog values can't be checked; the 8" flue and the outside-air option match. The catalog's height / width / depth equal the three numbers printed on Figure 6 'FOCUS ST Framing Example' (p. 12), which the manual says are larger than required; the text gives no unit dimensions and the figure doesn't say which number is which, so the catalog dimensions should be verified. p. 4 says the unit offers more than 500 square inches of pure fire viewing, while the website gives a glass viewing size of 288 in² (24 ¼" W x 11 ⅞" H); both are shown in specOptions and listed as a mismatch, though the manual doesn't say whether its figure covers one face or both of this two-sided unit. The website's Outside Air row (4", 5" also usable) leaves out the manual's 25' run limit for 4" duct; both shown in specAir. The website's BTU Maximum (50,000 BTU/hr) is wood heat output, which the manual doesn't give; the manual's 40,000 BTU/h is the maximum gas output allowed with a gas log set (p. 19), a different figure. Website rows the manual doesn't cover (shipping weight, firebox size, firewood length, door finish, mobile-home approval, BTU maximum, heating capacity, emissions rate) aren't shown; its Chimney, Gas logs and Warranty rows match the manual. The website's Outside Dimensions are the same three numbers as Figure 6 (see above), so no website note was added for them. p. 3 says to operate with the doors fully closed, while lighting and refuelling (p. 7) leave a door partly open / ajar for 3-10 minutes; both are shown, with a note in the safety, light and reload drawers (see conflicts). Figure 12 (p. 17) labels FO-FDM8 and FO-FDM7; the text names only FO-FDM8, which the guide uses. LM-8LAF is split across a line break on p. 17. Table 2 prints the 0 - 1000 ft straight value (12') on its own line; read as 12', matching Table 1 (D). Not transcribed (diagrams): Figure 1 clearances drawing, Figure 3 standoff positions, Figure 6 framing dimensions, Figure 13 custom spark guards, Figure 14 refractory brick order. Pages 21-23 (Complete Options List, Replacement Parts) have only headings in the text, so their tables/images weren't transcribed. The manual doesn't say whether the hearth extension and spark guard are needed on both faces of this two-sided unit. No troubleshooting code table, so codes is empty.
